q:
Consider the following statements:
1. Where a deadlock arises between the two Houses on an ordinary Bill, a joint sitting of both Houses may be summoned to resolve it.
2. The Constitution provides for a joint sitting of both Houses also in the case of a Money Bill.
Which of the statements is/are correct?

options.A: 1 only
options.B: 2 only
options.C: Both 1 and 2
options.D: Neither 1 nor 2

e: Under Article 108 a joint sitting can be summoned for an ordinary Bill deadlocked between the Houses. The Constitution makes no provision for a joint sitting for a Money Bill, so statement 1 alone is correct.

q: Which of the following correctly distinguishes the 'Main Cash Book' from the 'bank scroll' in railway accounts?

options.A: The Main Cash Book is the daily statement rendered by the bank, whereas the bank scroll is maintained in the Accounts Office
options.B: The Main Cash Book is the Railways' own record of cash receipts and payments, maintained chronologically in the Cash & Pay Office, whereas the bank scroll is the daily statement of receipts and payments rendered by the accredited bank, with reference to which the bank's transactions are reconciled with the railway books
options.C: Both the Main Cash Book and the bank scroll are maintained by the accredited bank
options.D: The Main Cash Book records only the earnings of stations, whereas the bank scroll records only the payments of the Cash & Pay Office

e: The Main Cash Book is the Railways own chronological record of cash receipts and payments kept in the Cash and Pay Office. The bank scroll is the daily statement rendered by the accredited bank, used to reconcile bank transactions with the books.

q: Which of the following correctly distinguishes the 'Budget Register' from the 'Main Cash Book' maintained in a railway Accounts Office?

options.A: The Budget Register records the day-to-day cash transactions, whereas the Main Cash Book watches the budget allotments
options.B: Both the registers record only the balances under the suspense heads
options.C: The Budget Register is maintained by the Cash & Pay Office, whereas the Main Cash Book is maintained by the Railway Board
options.D: The Budget Register records the budget allotments and the expenditure booked under each head, so that budgetary control is exercised over the expenditure, whereas the Main Cash Book records the cash receipts and payments of the railway chronologically

e: The Budget Register records budget allotments and expenditure booked under each head for budgetary control. The Main Cash Book records cash receipts and payments chronologically, so the two serve distinct purposes.

q: Which of the following correctly distinguishes an 'allotment' from an 'appropriation' in railway budgeting?

options.A: An allotment is the distribution of a grant voted by Parliament among the spending units and disbursing authorities for incurring expenditure, whereas an appropriation is the amount authorised through the Appropriation Act in respect of expenditure charged on the Consolidated Fund of India
options.B: An allotment is the amount authorised for charged expenditure, whereas an appropriation is the distribution of a grant among divisions
options.C: Both an allotment and an appropriation are voted by the Lok Sabha as Demands for Grants
options.D: An allotment can exceed the amount of the grant, whereas an appropriation is limited to the charged expenditure of the previous year

e: An allotment is the distribution of a grant voted by Parliament among spending units and disbursing authorities. An appropriation is the amount authorised by the Appropriation Act for expenditure charged on the Consolidated Fund of India.

q: Which of the following correctly distinguishes the 'Revised Estimates' from 'Supplementary Demands for Grants'?

options.A: The Revised Estimates are voted by Parliament during the year, whereas Supplementary Demands are not voted in any case
options.B: Both the Revised Estimates and the Supplementary Demands require a separate Appropriation Act
options.C: The Revised Estimates are a re-assessment, made during the year, of the likely receipts and expenditure for the year and are not separately voted by Parliament, whereas Supplementary Demands are presented to Parliament during the year to obtain additional grants where the sanctioned grant is insufficient or a new service is to be financed
options.D: The Revised Estimates relate only to the following year, whereas Supplementary Demands relate only to the previous year

e: Revised Estimates are a mid-year re-assessment of likely receipts and expenditure and are not separately voted. Supplementary Demands are presented and voted during the year when the grant is insufficient or a new service is to be financed.

q: The reports of the Departmentally Related Standing Committees of Parliament on the Demands for Grants are:

options.A: Presented to the Lok Sabha and also laid on the Table of the Rajya Sabha
options.B: Presented to the Rajya Sabha only
options.C: Submitted to the President for his assent
options.D: Sent directly to the Ministries concerned, without being presented to either House

e: Reports of Departmentally Related Standing Committees on Demands for Grants are presented to the Lok Sabha and also laid on the Table of the Rajya Sabha, since the committees have members from both Houses.

q: Which of the following correctly distinguishes 'Stores Suspense' from 'Manufacturing Suspense' in railway accounts?

options.A: Both the heads represent the cost of jobs in progress in workshops
options.B: The balance under Stores Suspense represents the value of the stores held in stock in the stores depots, whereas the balance under Manufacturing Suspense represents the cost of the jobs in progress in the workshops
options.C: The balance under Stores Suspense represents the cost of jobs in progress, whereas the balance under Manufacturing Suspense represents the value of stores in depots
options.D: Both the heads represent amounts recoverable from other railways on account of traffic transactions

e: The balance under Stores Suspense is the value of stores held in stock in depots. The balance under Manufacturing Suspense is the cost of jobs in progress in workshops, so the two suspense heads track different assets.

q: The reports of the Committee on Public Undertakings of Parliament are:

options.A: Presented to the Lok Sabha and also laid on the Table of the Rajya Sabha
options.B: Presented to the Rajya Sabha only
options.C: Submitted to the President of India
options.D: Presented to the Finance Minister alone

e: The Committee on Public Undertakings includes members from both Houses, so its reports are presented to the Lok Sabha and also laid on the Table of the Rajya Sabha.

q: Under Article 280 of the Constitution, besides recommending the distribution of taxes and the principles governing grants-in-aid, the Finance Commission also recommends:

options.A: The disinvestment programme of the Central Government
options.B: Any other matter referred to it by the President in the interests of sound finance
options.C: The rate of dividend payable by the Railways to the General Finances
options.D: The borrowing limits of the public sector undertakings

e: Under Article 280(3)(d), besides tax distribution and grants-in-aid principles, the Finance Commission recommends on any other matter referred to it by the President in the interests of sound finance.

q: Which of the following correctly distinguishes the 'Suspense Register' from the 'Budget Register' maintained in a railway Accounts Office?

options.A: The Suspense Register records the budget allotments, whereas the Budget Register records the outstanding suspense items
options.B: Both the registers record the sanctions and progressive expenditure on each work
options.C: The Suspense Register is maintained by the executive departments, whereas the Budget Register is maintained by the Audit Department
options.D: The Suspense Register watches the outstanding items under each suspense head, item-wise, till they are cleared to the final heads of account, whereas the Budget Register records the budget allotments and the expenditure booked under each head for the exercise of budgetary control

e: The Suspense Register watches outstanding items under each suspense head item-wise till clearance to final heads. The Budget Register records allotments and expenditure head-wise for budgetary control, which is a different function.

q: The opening debit balance under the head 'Cheques and Bills' of a railway is Rs 45,000. During the month, cheques and bills of Rs 6,20,000 are deposited with the bank and the bank intimates the realisation of cheques and bills of Rs 5,85,000. The closing debit balance under the head is:
e: Closing balance = opening Rs 45,000 + deposited Rs 6,20,000 - realised Rs 5,85,000 = Rs 80,000 debit, representing cheques and bills deposited but not yet realised.

q: The opening debit balance under the suspense head 'Demands Recoverable' of a railway is Rs 2,40,000. During the year, amounts of Rs 9,60,000 are debited to the head for services rendered to outside parties and Rs 10,20,000 are realised from the parties and credited to the head. The closing balance under the head is:

options.A: A credit balance of Rs 1,80,000
options.B: A debit balance of Rs 12,00,000
options.C: A debit balance of Rs 1,80,000
options.D: Nil, the head being closed at the end of the year

e: Closing balance = opening debit Rs 2,40,000 + debits Rs 9,60,000 - realisations credited Rs 10,20,000 = Rs 1,80,000 debit still recoverable from outside parties.

q: The opening debit balance under the remittance head 'Remittances into Banks' of a railway is Rs 1,25,000. During the month, remittances of Rs 14,75,000 are made into the bank and the bank gives credit for Rs 15,20,000. The closing balance under the head is:

options.A: A debit balance of Rs 80,000, representing the remittances still awaiting credit by the bank
options.B: A credit balance of Rs 80,000, representing amounts due to the bank
options.C: A debit balance of Rs 16,00,000
options.D: Nil, the head being squared off every month

e: Closing balance = opening debit Rs 1,25,000 + remittances Rs 14,75,000 - bank credit Rs 15,20,000 = Rs 80,000 debit, being remittances still awaiting credit by the bank.

q: The opening credit balance under the head 'Demands Payable' of a railway is Rs 3,60,000. During the year, amounts of Rs 12,40,000 are credited to the head for goods and services received and payments of Rs 13,00,000 are made and debited to the head. The closing balance under the head is:

options.A: A debit balance of Rs 3,00,000
options.B: A credit balance of Rs 16,00,000
options.C: Nil, all the liabilities having been discharged
options.D: A credit balance of Rs 3,00,000, representing the amounts still due to the parties for goods and services received

e: Closing balance = opening credit Rs 3,60,000 + credits for goods and services Rs 12,40,000 - payments debited Rs 13,00,000 = Rs 3,00,000 credit still due to parties.

q: The Block Account of a railway at the commencement of a year stands at Rs 48,000 crore. The capital outlay incurred during the year is Rs 3,200 crore and assets of the original cost of Rs 450 crore are sold and removed from the Block during the year. The Block Account at the close of the year stands at:

options.A: Rs 50,750 crore
options.B: Rs 51,200 crore
options.C: Rs 47,550 crore
options.D: Rs 44,350 crore

e: Closing Block Account = opening Rs 48,000 crore + capital outlay Rs 3,200 crore - original cost of assets sold and removed Rs 450 crore = Rs 50,750 crore.

q: The original appropriation for a charged service for a year is Rs 120 crore. During the year, a supplementary appropriation of Rs 15 crore is obtained for the service and charged provision of Rs 5 crore is surrendered. The Final Appropriation for the service is:

options.A: Rs 140 crore
options.B: Rs 110 crore
options.C: Rs 130 crore
options.D: Rs 120 crore

e: Final Appropriation = original Rs 120 crore + supplementary Rs 15 crore - surrendered Rs 5 crore = Rs 130 crore for the charged service.

q: An item of Rs 18,000, which should have been debited to an account in the Ledger, is posted to the credit side of that account, the amount itself being correct. The disagreement brought out in the Trial Balance on this account is:

options.B: Rs 36,000, the debits being short by Rs 18,000 and the credits being in excess by Rs 18,000
options.D: Nil, an error in posting to the wrong side being a compensating error

e: Posting Rs 18,000 to the credit side instead of the debit side makes debits short by Rs 18,000 and credits excess by Rs 18,000, so the Trial Balance disagrees by Rs 36,000, that is twice the amount.

q: Which of the following correctly distinguishes the 'Trial Balance' from the 'Balance Sheet' of a railway?

options.A: The Trial Balance exhibits the assets and liabilities of the Railways, whereas the Balance Sheet tests the arithmetical accuracy of the General Books
options.B: Both the Trial Balance and the Balance Sheet are statements of the assets and liabilities of the Railways
options.C: The Trial Balance is prepared only at the close of the financial year, whereas the Balance Sheet is extracted every month
options.D: The Trial Balance is the list of the balances extracted from the General Books to test the arithmetical accuracy of the accounts, whereas the Balance Sheet is the statement drawn up from the closed books exhibiting the assets and liabilities of the Railways

e: The Trial Balance is the list of balances from the General Books testing arithmetical accuracy. The Balance Sheet is the statement from the closed books exhibiting the assets and liabilities of the Railways.

q: Which of the following correctly distinguishes the 'Contingency Fund of India' from the 'Public Account of India'?

options.A: The Contingency Fund of India, forming Part II of the Government accounts, is a fund placed at the disposal of the President for meeting urgent unforeseen expenditure pending authorisation by Parliament, whereas the Public Account of India, forming Part III, holds moneys received by the Government in trust, such as provident funds and deposits, whose disbursement does not require appropriation by Parliament
options.B: The Contingency Fund of India is a part of the Public Account of India, and disbursements out of both require appropriation by Parliament
options.C: The Public Account of India is placed at the disposal of the President for unforeseen expenditure, whereas the Contingency Fund of India holds the provident fund balances of Government servants
options.D: Both the Contingency Fund of India and the Public Account of India form part of the Consolidated Fund of India

e: The Contingency Fund, in Part II, is at the disposal of the President for urgent unforeseen expenditure pending Parliament authorisation. The Public Account, in Part III, holds trust moneys like provident funds and deposits needing no appropriation.

q: Which of the following correctly distinguishes the Budget document 'Key Features of Budget' from the 'Key to Budget Documents'?

options.A: Both the documents contain the detailed head-wise estimates of expenditure of every Ministry
options.B: The 'Key Features of Budget' explains the various Budget documents and the terms used in them, whereas the 'Key to Budget Documents' presents the highlights of the Budget proposals
options.C: The 'Key Features of Budget' presents the highlights and salient features of the Budget proposals in a nutshell, whereas the 'Key to Budget Documents' explains the various Budget documents and the terms used in them
options.D: The 'Key Features of Budget' is laid only before the Rajya Sabha, whereas the 'Key to Budget Documents' is laid only before the Lok Sabha

e: Key Features of Budget presents the highlights and salient features of the Budget proposals in a nutshell. Key to Budget Documents explains the various Budget documents and the terms used in them.

q: Which of the following correctly distinguishes the 'Classified Abstract' from the 'Journal Book' of a railway?

options.A: The Classified Abstract records the transfer entries in chronological order, whereas the Journal Book summarises the transactions head-wise
options.B: The Classified Abstract is the head-wise summary of the month's transactions, compiled from the subsidiary books, from which the General Books are posted, whereas the Journal Book records the transfer (adjustment) entries in chronological order, entry by entry
options.C: Both the Classified Abstract and the Journal Book are rendered to the Railway Board as the monthly account of the railway
options.D: The Classified Abstract is maintained by the executive departments, whereas the Journal Book is maintained by the Audit Department

e: The Classified Abstract is the head-wise summary of the month transactions compiled from subsidiary books, from which the General Books are posted. The Journal Book records transfer entries chronologically, entry by entry.

q: Which of the following correctly distinguishes the 'Revenue Account' from the 'Balance Sheet' in the annual commercial accounts of the Railways?

options.A: The Revenue Account exhibits the earnings of the year against the working expenses of the year, so as to arrive at the net revenue or surplus, whereas the Balance Sheet exhibits the assets and liabilities of the Railways as they stand at the close of the year
options.B: The Revenue Account exhibits the assets and liabilities of the Railways, whereas the Balance Sheet exhibits the earnings and working expenses of the year
options.C: Both the Revenue Account and the Balance Sheet exhibit only the capital outlay of the Railways
options.D: The Revenue Account is a part of the Balance Sheet and shows the balances under the suspense heads alone

e: The Revenue Account matches the earnings of the year against working expenses to arrive at net revenue or surplus. The Balance Sheet exhibits the assets and liabilities of the Railways as at the close of the year.

q: Which of the following correctly distinguishes the Indian Railway Finance Code, Volume I, from the Indian Railway Finance Code, Volume II?

options.A: Volume I contains the lists of Major Heads and Primary Units of classification, whereas Volume II contains the rules of financial management
options.B: Both the volumes contain only the classification of accounts, in two alphabetical parts
options.C: Volume I deals with the purchase and custody of stores, whereas Volume II deals with Traffic Accounts
options.D: Volume I contains the rules and regulations governing the financial management of the Railways, including the delegation of financial powers and the budget procedure, whereas Volume II contains, in its appendices, the detailed classification of accounts — the lists of Major Heads, Sub-Major Heads, Minor Heads and Primary Units

e: Finance Code Volume I contains the rules of financial management, delegation of powers and budget procedure. Volume II contains in its appendices the classification of accounts - Major Heads, Sub-Major Heads, Minor Heads and Primary Units.

q: Which of the following correctly distinguishes a 'Vote on Account' from an 'Interim Budget'?

options.A: A Vote on Account is the Budget presented by an outgoing Government in an election year, whereas an Interim Budget is a grant voted for a part of the year
options.B: A Vote on Account is a grant voted by the Lok Sabha in advance for the initial part of a financial year, pending the completion of the budgetary process for the year, whereas an Interim Budget is the statement of the estimated receipts and expenditure presented by an outgoing Government in an election year, along with which a Vote on Account is taken for the initial part of the year pending the presentation of the regular Budget by the new Government
options.C: Both a Vote on Account and an Interim Budget are voted only by the Rajya Sabha
options.D: A Vote on Account requires no Appropriation Act, whereas an Interim Budget is itself an Appropriation Act

e: A Vote on Account is a grant voted in advance for the initial part of a year pending completion of the budget process. An Interim Budget is the estimates statement of an outgoing Government in an election year, with a Vote on Account taken alongside.

q: Which of the following correctly distinguishes the 'Debt Head Report' from the 'Balance Sheet' of a railway?

options.A: The Debt Head Report exhibits all the assets and liabilities of the Railways, whereas the Balance Sheet shows only the balances under the debt heads
options.B: Both the Debt Head Report and the Balance Sheet are rendered only at the close of the financial year
options.C: The Debt Head Report exhibits the balances outstanding under the debt, suspense and remittance heads, as recorded in the General Books, whereas the Balance Sheet is the annual statement of the assets and liabilities of the Railways, including the Block Account and the balances of the Railway Funds
options.D: The Debt Head Report is prepared by the Audit Department, whereas the Balance Sheet is prepared by the Cash & Pay Office

e: The Debt Head Report shows balances outstanding under debt, suspense and remittance heads in the General Books. The Balance Sheet is the annual statement of all assets and liabilities, including the Block Account and Railway Fund balances.

q: Which of the following correctly distinguishes the 'Pink Book' from the 'Rolling Stock Programme' of the Railways?

options.A: The Pink Book is the Works Programme, listing the works approved for inclusion in the year, arranged Plan Head-wise with the provision made for them, whereas the Rolling Stock Programme deals with the acquisition and renewal of locomotives, coaches, wagons and other rolling stock
options.B: The Pink Book deals with the acquisition of rolling stock, whereas the Rolling Stock Programme lists the civil engineering works of the year
options.C: Both the Pink Book and the Rolling Stock Programme are registers maintained in the Accounts Office for recording expenditure
options.D: The Pink Book is prepared by the stores department, whereas the Rolling Stock Programme is prepared by the Traffic Accounts Office

e: The Pink Book is the Works Programme listing works approved for the year Plan Head-wise with provisions. The Rolling Stock Programme separately deals with acquisition and renewal of locomotives, coaches, wagons and other rolling stock.

q: Which of the following correctly distinguishes the 'Earnings Budget' from the 'Working Expenses Budget' of the Railways?

options.A: Both the Earnings Budget and the Working Expenses Budget are framed by the Accounts Department alone, without reference to the executive departments
options.B: The Earnings Budget estimates the expenditure on works, whereas the Working Expenses Budget estimates the traffic expected during the year
options.C: The Earnings Budget is voted by Parliament, whereas the Working Expenses Budget is not shown to Parliament at all
options.D: The Earnings Budget contains the estimates of the earnings expected from coaching, goods and sundry other traffic, framed on the basis of the traffic anticipated, whereas the Working Expenses Budget contains the estimates of the ordinary working expenses, including the appropriations to the Depreciation Reserve Fund and the Pension Fund charged to revenue

e: The Earnings Budget estimates earnings from coaching, goods and sundry traffic based on anticipated traffic. The Working Expenses Budget estimates ordinary working expenses, including appropriations to the Depreciation Reserve Fund and Pension Fund.

q: Which of the following correctly distinguishes a 'Transfer Certificate' from a 'Cash Remittance Note' in railway accounts?

options.A: A Transfer Certificate accompanies the earnings remitted by a station, whereas a Cash Remittance Note intimates an inter-railway transfer debit
options.B: A Transfer Certificate is the advice by which one railway intimates a transfer debit or credit raised against another railway, whereas a Cash Remittance Note is the document which accompanies the earnings remitted by a station to the Cash Office or the bank, with reference to which the remittance is checked
options.C: Both the documents are issued by the Reserve Bank of India for the settlement of Government balances
options.D: A Transfer Certificate is used only for cash transactions, whereas a Cash Remittance Note is used only for book adjustments

e: A Transfer Certificate is the advice by which one railway intimates a transfer debit or credit against another railway. A Cash Remittance Note accompanies earnings remitted by a station to the Cash Office or bank for checking the remittance.

q: Which of the following correctly distinguishes an 'Advice of Payment' from a 'Transfer Certificate' in railway accounts?

options.A: Both the documents intimate inter-railway traffic debits raised through the Traffic Book
options.B: An Advice of Payment is issued by the Reserve Bank of India, whereas a Transfer Certificate is issued by the accredited bank
options.C: An Advice of Payment is sent by an accounting unit which has made a payment on behalf of another accounting unit, so that the latter can bring the expenditure to account under its own final head, whereas a Transfer Certificate intimates a transfer debit or credit raised by one railway against another railway in an inter-railway transfer transaction
options.D: An Advice of Payment intimates a debit raised by one railway against another, whereas a Transfer Certificate intimates a payment made on behalf of another Ministry

e: An Advice of Payment is sent by a unit that paid on behalf of another unit so the latter can book the expenditure under its own final head. A Transfer Certificate intimates an inter-railway transfer debit or credit.

q: Which of the following correctly distinguishes 'Demands Recoverable' from 'Traffic Suspense' in railway accounts?

options.A: 'Demands Recoverable' represents amounts due to the Railways from outside parties for goods supplied or services rendered, pending realisation, whereas 'Traffic Suspense' represents debits raised against stations or other railways, such as disallowances and undercharges on traffic transactions, pending recovery or final adjustment
options.B: 'Demands Recoverable' represents traffic debits raised against stations, whereas 'Traffic Suspense' represents amounts due from outside parties for services rendered
options.C: Both the heads represent deposits received from contractors, pending refund
options.D: 'Demands Recoverable' is a remittance head, whereas 'Traffic Suspense' is an earnings head

e: Demands Recoverable are amounts due from outside parties for goods supplied or services rendered, pending realisation. Traffic Suspense holds traffic debits like disallowances and undercharges against stations or railways pending adjustment.

q: Which of the following correctly distinguishes 'Cheques and Bills' from 'PSB Suspense' in railway accounts?

options.A: Both the heads record the transactions of the Railways with the Reserve Bank of India alone
options.B: 'Cheques and Bills' is operated for the transactions of the accredited bank pending its advice, whereas 'PSB Suspense' is operated for cheques deposited with the bank
options.C: 'Cheques and Bills' represents amounts due from stations on traffic transactions, whereas 'PSB Suspense' represents cheques issued but unpaid
options.D: 'Cheques and Bills' is operated for cheques and bills received and deposited with the bank, pending realisation, and for cheques issued, whereas 'PSB Suspense' is operated for the transactions of the accredited public sector bank, pending receipt of the bank's advice and adjustment to the final heads of account

e: Cheques and Bills covers cheques and bills received, deposited with the bank pending realisation, and cheques issued. PSB Suspense covers transactions of the accredited public sector bank pending its advice and adjustment to final heads.

q: Which of the following correctly distinguishes the 'Development Fund' from the 'Railway Safety Fund' of the Railways?

options.A: Both the funds are fed by the safety surcharge levied on passenger fares
options.B: The Development Fund is fed by appropriations made out of the surplus (net revenue) of the Railways and is used for passenger amenities, labour welfare and unremunerative operational improvement works, whereas the Railway Safety Fund is fed mainly by the safety surcharge levied on passenger fares and is used for works of road safety at level crossings and for road over-bridges and road under-bridges
options.C: The Development Fund is fed by the safety surcharge on passenger fares, whereas the Railway Safety Fund is fed out of the surplus of the Railways
options.D: The Development Fund is used for renewals and replacements of track, whereas the Railway Safety Fund is used for staff welfare works

e: The Development Fund is fed from the Railways surplus and used for passenger amenities, labour welfare and unremunerative improvements. The Railway Safety Fund is fed mainly by the safety surcharge on fares and used for level crossing and road bridge safety works.

q: Which of the following correctly distinguishes the 'Stores Budget' from the 'Earnings Budget' of the Railways?

options.A: The Stores Budget is framed on the basis of the traffic anticipated during the year, whereas the Earnings Budget is framed on the requirements of the consuming departments
options.B: Both the budgets are derived budgets, framed from the Works Programme alone
options.C: The Stores Budget is a derived budget, framed on the basis of the requirements of the consuming departments and the programme of works, whereas the Earnings Budget is framed on the basis of the traffic anticipated during the year, as estimated by the executive departments
options.D: The Stores Budget is voted by Parliament as a separate Demand, whereas the Earnings Budget forms part of the Works Programme

e: The Stores Budget is a derived budget framed from the requirements of consuming departments and the works programme. The Earnings Budget is framed on the traffic anticipated during the year as estimated by the executive departments.

q: Which of the following correctly distinguishes the 'Liability Register' from the 'Suspense Register' maintained in a railway Accounts Office?

options.A: The Liability Register records the liabilities and commitments incurred against the budget allotments, so that the funds required for meeting them are kept in view, whereas the Suspense Register watches, item-wise, the amounts outstanding under each suspense head till they are cleared to the final heads of account
options.B: The Liability Register watches the outstanding items under the suspense heads, whereas the Suspense Register records the commitments incurred against the allotments
options.C: Both the registers record the budget allotments as modified by re-appropriation
options.D: The Liability Register is maintained by the Audit Department, whereas the Suspense Register is maintained by the executive departments

e: The Liability Register records liabilities and commitments against budget allotments so funds needed are kept in view. The Suspense Register watches item-wise the amounts outstanding under suspense heads till they are cleared.

q: Which of the following correctly distinguishes the 'Works Register' from the 'Debt Head Report' of a railway?

options.A: Both the documents exhibit the balances outstanding under the debt, suspense and remittance heads
options.B: The Works Register exhibits the balances under the debt heads, whereas the Debt Head Report records the expenditure on each work
options.C: The Works Register is rendered to the Railway Board as the monthly account, whereas the Debt Head Report is an internal register of the executive departments
options.D: The Works Register is maintained in the Accounts Office and records, work-wise, the expenditure incurred on each sanctioned work against its sanctioned estimate, whereas the Debt Head Report exhibits the balances outstanding under the debt, suspense and remittance heads as recorded in the General Books

e: The Works Register records work-wise expenditure on each sanctioned work against its sanctioned estimate. The Debt Head Report exhibits balances outstanding under debt, suspense and remittance heads as in the General Books.

q: Which of the following correctly distinguishes 'Demands Payable' from 'Deposits' in railway accounts?

options.A: Both the heads represent advances made by the Railways to outside parties, pending recovery
options.B: 'Demands Payable' represents amounts due by the Railways to outside parties for goods and services received, pending payment, whereas 'Deposits' represents amounts received from parties, such as earnest money and security deposits, which are held by the Railways and are repayable or adjustable to the parties concerned
options.C: 'Demands Payable' represents moneys received from parties and held by the Railways, whereas 'Deposits' represents amounts due for goods received
options.D: 'Demands Payable' is an earnings head, whereas 'Deposits' is a suspense head for traffic transactions

e: Demands Payable are amounts due to outside parties for goods and services received, pending payment. Deposits are amounts received from parties, like earnest money and security deposits, held by the Railways and repayable or adjustable.

q: Which of the following correctly distinguishes 'PAO Suspense' from 'PSB Suspense' in railway accounts?

options.A: Both the heads record the transactions of the Railways with the Pay and Accounts Offices of other Ministries
options.B: 'PAO Suspense' is operated for the transactions of the accredited bank, whereas 'PSB Suspense' is operated for transactions with other Ministries
options.C: 'PAO Suspense' is operated for transactions with the Pay and Accounts Offices of other Ministries and Departments, pending settlement, whereas 'PSB Suspense' is operated for the transactions of the accredited public sector bank, pending receipt of the bank's advice and adjustment in the railway books
options.D: 'PAO Suspense' represents cheques deposited with the bank but not realised, whereas 'PSB Suspense' represents station earnings in transit

e: PAO Suspense covers transactions with Pay and Accounts Offices of other Ministries and Departments pending settlement. PSB Suspense covers transactions of the accredited public sector bank pending its advice and adjustment in railway books.

q: Which of the following correctly distinguishes the 'focal point' system from 'CIPS' in the railway remittance and payment arrangements?

options.A: Under the focal point system, the earnings of a group of stations are remitted to, and accounted at, nominated focal point branches of the accredited bank, whereas CIPS is the arrangement for the centralised electronic payment of bills and other payments of the Railways through the accredited bank
options.B: The focal point system is an arrangement for the payment of suppliers' bills, whereas CIPS is an arrangement for the collection of station earnings
options.C: Both the focal point system and CIPS are systems for the apportionment of earnings among the zonal railways
options.D: The focal point system is operated by the Reserve Bank of India at Nagpur, whereas CIPS is operated by the stations themselves

e: Under the focal point system, earnings of a group of stations are remitted to and accounted at nominated focal point branches of the accredited bank. CIPS is the centralised electronic payment system for bills and other railway payments.

q: Which of the following correctly distinguishes 'IPAS' from 'e-Kuber'?

options.A: IPAS is the core banking solution of the Reserve Bank of India, whereas e-Kuber is the payroll application of the Railways
options.B: Both IPAS and e-Kuber are applications maintained by the Railways for the reservation of passenger accommodation
options.C: IPAS is used for the apportionment of earnings in the Traffic Book, whereas e-Kuber is used for the payment of suppliers' bills by the zonal railways alone
options.D: IPAS is the integrated application of the Railways for payroll and accounts work, whereas e-Kuber is the core banking solution of the Reserve Bank of India through which Government receipts and payments handled by the Reserve Bank are processed and accounted

e: IPAS is the Railways integrated application for payroll and accounts work. E-Kuber is the core banking solution of the Reserve Bank of India through which Government receipts and payments handled by the Bank are processed.

q: Which of the following correctly distinguishes 'PFMS' from 'Bharatkosh'?

options.A: PFMS is the portal for depositing the non-tax receipts of the Government, whereas Bharatkosh is the platform for monitoring the flow of funds under Government schemes
options.B: PFMS is a central platform for payment, accounting and monitoring of the flow of Government funds, including releases under Government schemes, whereas Bharatkosh is the Non-Tax Receipt Portal providing a single-window facility for depositing the non-tax receipts of the Government of India electronically
options.C: Both PFMS and Bharatkosh are applications of the Railways for the compilation of the monthly Account Current
options.D: PFMS is maintained by the Reserve Bank of India, whereas Bharatkosh is maintained by the Railway Board

e: PFMS is the central platform for payment, accounting and monitoring of Government fund flows, including scheme releases. Bharatkosh is the Non-Tax Receipt Portal for depositing non-tax receipts of the Government of India electronically.

q: Which of the following correctly distinguishes the 'Outcome Budget' from the 'Expenditure Profile' presented with the Union Budget?

options.A: Both the documents present the detailed Demands for Grants of the Ministries, head-wise
options.B: The Outcome Budget presents a broad snapshot of the total expenditure of the Government, whereas the Expenditure Profile relates the outlays to the outcomes expected
options.C: The Outcome Budget seeks to relate the financial outlays provided for the schemes and programmes to the outcomes and deliverables expected from them, whereas the Expenditure Profile presents a broad snapshot of the pattern of the total expenditure of the Government, ministry-wise and scheme-wise
options.D: The Outcome Budget is prepared by the Comptroller and Auditor General of India, whereas the Expenditure Profile is prepared by the zonal railways

e: The Outcome Budget relates financial outlays on schemes and programmes to the outcomes and deliverables expected. The Expenditure Profile gives a broad snapshot of total expenditure, ministry-wise and scheme-wise.

q: Which of the following correctly distinguishes the 'Annual Financial Statement' from the 'Demands for Grants'?

options.A: The Annual Financial Statement is the statement of the estimated receipts and expenditure of the Government for the year, laid before both Houses of Parliament, whereas the Demands for Grants present the estimates of expenditure, ministry-wise, which are submitted to the vote of the Lok Sabha alone
options.B: The Annual Financial Statement presents only the estimates of expenditure, whereas the Demands for Grants present the estimates of receipts and expenditure
options.C: Both the Annual Financial Statement and the Demands for Grants are voted by the Lok Sabha
options.D: The Annual Financial Statement is presented only to the Rajya Sabha, whereas the Demands for Grants are presented only to the President

e: The Annual Financial Statement under Article 112 shows estimated receipts and expenditure and is laid before both Houses. Demands for Grants show expenditure estimates ministry-wise and are submitted to the vote of the Lok Sabha alone.

q: Which of the following correctly distinguishes the 'Public Accounts Committee' from the 'Estimates Committee' of Parliament?

options.A: Both the Committees examine the estimates of the Ministries before the Demands for Grants are voted
options.B: The Public Accounts Committee examines the estimates for economy, whereas the Estimates Committee examines the Appropriation Accounts of past years
options.C: The Public Accounts Committee consists of members of the Lok Sabha alone, whereas the Estimates Committee consists of members of both Houses
options.D: The Public Accounts Committee examines, after the expenditure has been incurred, the Appropriation Accounts and the audit reports of the Comptroller and Auditor General thereon, whereas the Estimates Committee examines the estimates of the Ministries with a view to suggesting economies and improvements in organisation and efficiency consistent with the policy underlying the estimates

e: The Public Accounts Committee examines, after expenditure, the Appropriation Accounts and CAG audit reports on them. The Estimates Committee examines estimates beforehand to suggest economies and improvements consistent with the underlying policy.

q: Which of the following correctly distinguishes the 'Estimates Committee' from the 'Departmentally Related Standing Committee on Railways'?

options.A: The Estimates Committee examines the Demands for Grants of the Ministry of Railways alone, whereas the Standing Committee on Railways examines the estimates of all the Ministries
options.B: The Estimates Committee examines the estimates of such Ministries, departments or subjects as it selects for examination and reports on the economies and improvements that can be effected, whereas the Departmentally Related Standing Committee on Railways examines the Demands for Grants of the Ministry of Railways before they are voted and presents a report which is recommendatory in character
options.C: Both the Committees vote the Demands for Grants after examining them
options.D: The Estimates Committee is a committee of both Houses of Parliament, whereas the Standing Committee on Railways is a committee of the Rajya Sabha alone

e: The Estimates Committee selects Ministries, departments or subjects and reports on economies and organisational improvements. The Standing Committee on Railways examines the Railway Demands before voting and its report is recommendatory.

q: Which of the following correctly distinguishes an 'Exceptional Grant' from an 'Excess Grant'?

options.A: Both an Exceptional Grant and an Excess Grant are voted after the close of the year to regularise excess expenditure
options.B: An Exceptional Grant regularises expenditure already incurred in excess of a grant, whereas an Excess Grant is made for a special purpose of the current year
options.C: An Exceptional Grant is made for a special purpose which does not form part of the current services of the financial year, whereas an Excess Grant is voted after the close of the year to regularise expenditure already incurred in excess of the amount granted for a service
options.D: An Exceptional Grant is voted by the Rajya Sabha, whereas an Excess Grant is voted by the Lok Sabha

e: An Exceptional Grant under Article 116 is for a special purpose not forming part of the current services of the year. An Excess Grant is voted after the year to regularise expenditure already incurred beyond a grant.

q: Which of the following correctly distinguishes a 'token grant' from a 'token cut'?

options.A: A token grant is a nominal grant taken to obtain the approval of Parliament for a new service whose cost can be met by re-appropriation within the grant, whereas a token cut is a cut motion moved on a Demand for Grant to ventilate a specific grievance, proposing a nominal reduction in the amount of the Demand
options.B: A token grant is a cut motion proposing a nominal reduction in a Demand, whereas a token cut is a grant taken for a new service
options.C: Both a token grant and a token cut are devices for regularising excess expenditure after the close of the year
options.D: A token grant dispenses with the approval of Parliament for a new service, whereas a token cut is moved only in the Rajya Sabha

e: A token grant is a nominal grant to get Parliament approval for a new service whose cost is met by re-appropriation within the grant. A token cut is a cut motion proposing a nominal reduction to ventilate a specific grievance.

q: Which of the following correctly distinguishes 'Stores Suspense' from the 'Stores Budget' of the Railways?

options.A: Both Stores Suspense and the Stores Budget record the value of the stores held in stock in the depots
options.B: Stores Suspense is a derived budget of stores purchases, whereas the Stores Budget is the head under which stores are held in stock
options.C: The balance under Stores Suspense is voted by Parliament every year, whereas the Stores Budget is a suspense head of account
options.D: Stores Suspense is the head of account under which the stores received into the stock of the depots are held, its debit balance representing the value of the stores in stock, whereas the Stores Budget is the derived budget of the stores requirements, framed on the basis of the requirements of the consuming departments and the programme of works

e: Stores Suspense is the head under which stores received into depot stock are held, its debit balance being the value of stores in stock. The Stores Budget is the derived budget of stores requirements from consuming departments and works programme.

q: Which of the following correctly distinguishes the 'Capital Account' from the 'Balance Sheet' in the annual commercial accounts of the Railways?

options.A: The Capital Account exhibits all the assets and liabilities of the Railways, whereas the Balance Sheet exhibits only the capital outlay of the year
options.B: The Capital Account exhibits the capital outlay of the Railways and the assets created out of it, as reflected in the Block Account, whereas the Balance Sheet exhibits the assets and liabilities of the Railways as a whole, including the Block Account, the balances of the Railway Funds and the balances under the debt, suspense and remittance heads
options.C: Both the Capital Account and the Balance Sheet exhibit the earnings and working expenses of the year
options.D: The Capital Account is prepared by the Audit Department, whereas the Balance Sheet is prepared by the executive departments

e: The Capital Account shows capital outlay and assets created, as in the Block Account. The Balance Sheet shows assets and liabilities as a whole, including the Block Account, Railway Fund balances and debt, suspense and remittance balances.

q:
Consider the following statements about the Finance Commission:
1. The members of the Finance Commission hold office for such period as may be specified by the President in the order of appointment.
2. A member of the Finance Commission is eligible for reappointment as a member of the Commission.
Which of the statements is/are correct?

options.A: 1 only
options.B: 2 only
options.C: Both 1 and 2
options.D: Neither 1 nor 2

e: Under the Finance Commission Act and Article 280, members hold office for the period specified by the President in the appointment order, and a member is eligible for reappointment. Both statements are correct.

q: The reports of the Comptroller and Auditor General of India relating to the accounts of a State are submitted, under Article 151 of the Constitution, to:

options.A: The Governor of the State, who causes them to be laid before the Legislature of the State
options.B: The President of India, in the same manner as the reports relating to the accounts of the Union
options.C: The Chief Minister of the State
options.D: The Speaker of the State Legislative Assembly directly

e: Under Article 151(2), CAG reports relating to the accounts of a State are submitted to the Governor of the State, who causes them to be laid before the Legislature of the State.

q: A State Government, a part of whose loan raised earlier by the Union Government, or guaranteed by it, is still outstanding, proposes to raise a fresh loan in the market. Under Article 293 of the Constitution, the State:

options.A: Can raise the loan freely, the borrowing power of a State being unrestricted while its Legislature is in session
options.B: Can raise the loan only with the sanction of the Reserve Bank of India
options.C: Must first obtain the approval of its State Finance Commission
options.D: Cannot raise the loan without the consent of the Government of India, which may impose such conditions as it thinks fit in granting the consent

e: Under Article 293(3), a State with any part of a loan raised or guaranteed by the Government of India still outstanding cannot raise a fresh loan without the consent of the Government of India, which may impose conditions.

q:
Consider the following statements:
1. A surcharge levied by the Union for the purposes of the Union, under Article 271 of the Constitution, is not part of the divisible pool of taxes shared with the States.
2. The proceeds of such a surcharge are shared with the States in the same manner as the net proceeds of the shareable Union taxes.
Which of the statements is/are correct?

options.A: 1 only
options.B: 2 only
options.C: Both 1 and 2
options.D: Neither 1 nor 2

e: Under Articles 269 and 271, a surcharge levied by the Union for Union purposes forms no part of the divisible pool shared with States, so statement 1 is correct and statement 2 is wrong.

q: For the purposes of the transaction of Government business in the Ministry of Railways, the Financial Commissioner (Railways), who is a Member of the Railway Board and its principal financial adviser, also functions as:

options.A: The head of the Railway Audit organisation
options.B: The Chairman of the Indian Railway Finance Corporation
options.C: Ex-officio Secretary to the Government of India in the Ministry of Railways
options.D: An officer of the Ministry of Finance deputed to conduct the internal check of railway expenditure

e: The Financial Commissioner (Railways) is a Member of the Railway Board, its principal financial adviser, and also functions as ex-officio Secretary to the Government of India in the Ministry of Railways.

q: A public sector undertaking of the Railways in which the Central Government holds seventy per cent of the paid-up share capital is a 'Government company', because a Government company is one in which:

options.A: All the shares are held by the Government or by Government servants
options.B: Not less than fifty-one per cent of the paid-up share capital is held by the Central Government, or by a State Government, or partly by the one and partly by the other
options.C: The Chairman and all the Directors are appointed by the Government
options.D: The accounts are audited by the Comptroller and Auditor General of India in every case

e: Under Section 2(45) of the Companies Act 2013, a Government company is one where not less than 51 percent of the paid-up share capital is held by the Central Government, a State Government, or partly by both. Seventy percent clearly qualifies.

q: A Money Bill, after being passed by the Lok Sabha, is transmitted to the Rajya Sabha, which returns it within fourteen days with recommendations. The Lok Sabha does not accept the recommendations of the Rajya Sabha. The position is that:

options.A: The Bill lapses and has to be introduced afresh in the Lok Sabha
options.B: A joint sitting of both Houses is summoned to resolve the disagreement
options.C: The Bill is sent to the President, who returns it to the Lok Sabha for reconsideration
options.D: The Bill is deemed to have been passed by both Houses in the form in which it was passed by the Lok Sabha, without the recommendations of the Rajya Sabha

e: Under Article 109, if the Lok Sabha does not accept Rajya Sabha recommendations on a Money Bill returned within 14 days, the Bill is deemed passed by both Houses in the form passed by the Lok Sabha.

q: Which of the following correctly distinguishes the duties referred to in Article 268 of the Constitution from the taxes referred to in Article 269?

options.A: The duties under Article 268 are levied and collected by the States themselves, whereas the taxes under Article 269 are shared between the Union and the States
options.B: The duties under Article 268 are levied by the Union but collected and appropriated by the States, whereas the taxes under Article 269 are levied and collected by the Union but assigned wholly to the States, their proceeds not forming part of the Consolidated Fund of India
options.C: Both the duties under Article 268 and the taxes under Article 269 are levied, collected and retained by the Union alone
options.D: The duties under Article 268 are assigned to the States by the Finance Commission, whereas the taxes under Article 269 are levied by the States and collected by the Union

e: Duties under Article 268, like stamp duties, are levied by the Union but collected and appropriated by the States. Taxes under Article 269 are levied and collected by the Union but assigned wholly to the States, outside the Consolidated Fund of India.

q: A question arises as to the amount of the net proceeds of a shareable Union tax in a year, the net proceeds being the gross proceeds reduced by the cost of collection. The amount is finally determined on the basis of:

options.A: The figures worked out by the Budget Division of the Ministry of Finance
options.B: The recommendations of the Finance Commission for that year
options.C: The calculation and certificate of the Comptroller and Auditor General of India, whose certificate is final
options.D: The report of the Public Accounts Committee on the Finance Accounts

e: Under Article 279, net proceeds means gross proceeds less cost of collection, and the amount is ascertained and certified by the Comptroller and Auditor General of India, whose certificate is final.

q: Which of the following correctly distinguishes the salaries and allowances of the Judges of a High Court from the pensions payable to or in respect of such Judges?

options.A: The salaries and allowances of the Judges of a High Court are charged on the Consolidated Fund of the State, whereas the pensions payable to or in respect of them are charged on the Consolidated Fund of India
options.B: Both the salaries and the pensions of the Judges of a High Court are charged on the Consolidated Fund of India
options.C: The salaries of the Judges of a High Court are charged on the Consolidated Fund of India, whereas their pensions are charged on the Consolidated Fund of the State
options.D: Both the salaries and the pensions of the Judges of a High Court are submitted to the annual vote of the State Legislature

e: Salaries and allowances of High Court Judges are charged on the Consolidated Fund of the State under Article 202(3), while pensions payable to or in respect of them are charged on the Consolidated Fund of India under Article 112(3).

q: On the basis of the recommendations of the State Finance Commission, the measures needed to augment the Consolidated Fund of a State in order to supplement the resources of the Panchayats and the Municipalities in the State are recommended to the President by:

options.A: The Comptroller and Auditor General of India
options.B: The State Finance Commission itself, directly to the President
options.C: The Ministry of Panchayati Raj
options.D: The Finance Commission constituted under Article 280 of the Constitution

e: Under Article 280(3)(bb) and (c), it is the Union Finance Commission that recommends, on the basis of State Finance Commission recommendations, measures to augment a State Consolidated Fund to supplement Panchayat and Municipality resources.

q: The duties and powers of the Comptroller and Auditor General of India in relation to the audit of the accounts of the Union, the States and other authorities are such as may be prescribed by or under a law made in this behalf by:

options.A: The President, under Article 150 of the Constitution
options.B: Parliament, as contemplated by Article 149 of the Constitution
options.C: The Public Accounts Committee, through its reports
options.D: The Finance Commission, under Article 280 of the Constitution

e: Under Article 149, the duties and powers of the CAG in relation to audit of the Union, States and other authorities are as prescribed by or under a law made by Parliament.

q: The Trial Balance extracted from the General Books of a railway does not agree, and the difference cannot be located immediately, the accounts having to be closed. Pending the location and rectification of the error, the difference is:

options.A: Written off to the working expenses of the year
options.B: Carried to the Balance Sheet as a permanent asset of the Railways
options.C: Placed to a Suspense Account, so that the Trial Balance is made to agree, and cleared when the error is located and rectified
options.D: Adjusted against the balance under 'Deposits with Reserve Bank'

e: When a Trial Balance difference cannot be located immediately, it is placed to a Suspense Account so the books can be closed and the Trial Balance made to agree, and is cleared when the error is found and rectified.

q: A Parliamentary committee which examines the Demands for Grants of the Ministry of Railways before they are voted has thirty-one members, twenty-one drawn from the Lok Sabha and ten from the Rajya Sabha, nominated by the Speaker and the Chairman of the Rajya Sabha respectively. The committee is the:

options.A: Departmentally Related Standing Committee on Railways
options.B: Estimates Committee of Parliament
options.C: Railway Convention Committee
options.D: Committee on Public Undertakings

e: The committee described, with 31 members - 21 from Lok Sabha and 10 from Rajya Sabha nominated by the Speaker and Chairman - examining Railway Demands before voting, is the Departmentally Related Standing Committee on Railways.

q: A Member of Parliament wishes to know what progress has been made in implementing the announcements made in the Budget of the previous year. The Budget document which specifically reports this is the:

options.A: Expenditure Profile
options.B: Outcome Budget
options.C: Key to Budget Documents
options.D: Document on the Implementation of Budget Announcements

e: Progress on implementing the previous Budget announcements is specifically reported in the separate Budget document titled Implementation of Budget Announcements, distinct from the Expenditure Profile or Outcome Budget.

q: Which of the following correctly distinguishes the Finance Commission of a State from the Finance Commission of the Union?

options.A: Both the Commissions are constituted by the President under Article 280 of the Constitution
options.B: The State Finance Commission is constituted by the Governor under Article 243-I of the Constitution to review the financial position of the Panchayats and the Municipalities, whereas the Union Finance Commission is constituted by the President under Article 280 to recommend the distribution of taxes between the Union and the States and the principles governing grants-in-aid
options.C: The State Finance Commission recommends the distribution of taxes between the Union and the States, whereas the Union Finance Commission reviews the finances of the Panchayats
options.D: The State Finance Commission is constituted by the President, whereas the Union Finance Commission is constituted by the Governor of each State in turn

e: The State Finance Commission is constituted by the Governor under Article 243-I to review Panchayat and Municipality finances. The Union Finance Commission is constituted by the President under Article 280 for tax distribution and grants-in-aid.

q: The fiscal deficit of the Government for a year is Rs 9,00,000 crore and the interest payments during the year amount to Rs 3,50,000 crore. The primary deficit of the Government for the year is:

options.A: Rs 12,50,000 crore
options.B: Rs 9,00,000 crore
options.C: Rs 5,50,000 crore
options.D: Nil, a primary deficit arising only when there is a revenue deficit

e: Primary deficit = fiscal deficit - interest payments = Rs 9,00,000 crore - Rs 3,50,000 crore = Rs 5,50,000 crore.

q: The revenue deficit of the Government for a year is Rs 2,40,000 crore, and the grants-in-aid given during the year for the creation of capital assets amount to Rs 60,000 crore. The Effective Revenue Deficit for the year is:

options.A: Rs 1,80,000 crore
options.B: Rs 2,40,000 crore
options.C: Rs 3,00,000 crore
options.D: Rs 60,000 crore

e: Effective Revenue Deficit = revenue deficit - grants for creation of capital assets = Rs 2,40,000 crore - Rs 60,000 crore = Rs 1,80,000 crore.

q: The capital expenditure of the Government for a year is Rs 3,00,000 crore and the grants-in-aid given during the year for the creation of capital assets amount to Rs 50,000 crore. The Effective Capital Expenditure for the year is:

options.A: Rs 2,50,000 crore
options.B: Rs 3,00,000 crore
options.C: Rs 50,000 crore
options.D: Rs 3,50,000 crore

e: Effective Capital Expenditure = capital expenditure + grants for creation of capital assets = Rs 3,00,000 crore + Rs 50,000 crore = Rs 3,50,000 crore.

q: Which of the following correctly distinguishes the Medium-Term Fiscal Policy Statement from the Macro-Economic Framework Statement laid before Parliament under the FRBM Act?

options.A: Both the statements set out three-year rolling targets for the fiscal indicators of the Government
options.B: The Medium-Term Fiscal Policy Statement sets out three-year rolling targets for specified fiscal indicators, whereas the Macro-Economic Framework Statement sets out an assessment of the growth prospects of the economy along with the specific underlying assumptions
options.C: The Medium-Term Fiscal Policy Statement assesses the growth prospects of the economy, whereas the Macro-Economic Framework Statement sets out the rolling targets for fiscal indicators
options.D: The Medium-Term Fiscal Policy Statement is prepared by the Comptroller and Auditor General of India, whereas the Macro-Economic Framework Statement is prepared by the Reserve Bank of India

e: Under the FRBM Act, the Medium-Term Fiscal Policy Statement sets three-year rolling targets for specified fiscal indicators, while the Macro-Economic Framework Statement assesses growth prospects of the economy with its underlying assumptions.

q: Which of the following correctly distinguishes the Fiscal Policy Strategy Statement from the Medium-Term Expenditure Framework Statement laid before Parliament under the FRBM Act?

options.A: The Fiscal Policy Strategy Statement sets out the expenditure projections of the Ministries for three years, whereas the Medium-Term Expenditure Framework Statement sets out the strategic priorities of the Government in the fiscal area
options.B: Both the statements are presented only in the session following the Budget session
options.C: The Fiscal Policy Strategy Statement sets out the strategic priorities of the Government in the fiscal area for the ensuing financial year, whereas the Medium-Term Expenditure Framework Statement sets out the expenditure projections of the Ministries for three years
options.D: The Fiscal Policy Strategy Statement is voted by Parliament, whereas the Medium-Term Expenditure Framework Statement is laid only before the Rajya Sabha

e: Under the FRBM Act, the Fiscal Policy Strategy Statement sets out the strategic priorities of the Government in the fiscal area for the ensuing year, while the Medium-Term Expenditure Framework Statement gives three-year expenditure projections of Ministries.

q: Which of the following correctly distinguishes the Annual Financial Statement from the Finance Accounts of the Railways?

options.A: The Annual Financial Statement is the statement of the estimated receipts and expenditure of the year, laid before both Houses of Parliament, whereas the Finance Accounts present the actual receipts and disbursements of the completed year, classified under the Major Heads of account
options.B: The Annual Financial Statement presents the actual accounts of the completed year, whereas the Finance Accounts present the estimates for the ensuing year
options.C: Both the Annual Financial Statement and the Finance Accounts are voted by the Lok Sabha
options.D: The Annual Financial Statement is compiled by the Comptroller and Auditor General of India, whereas the Finance Accounts are presented by the Finance Minister

e: The Annual Financial Statement shows estimated receipts and expenditure for the year and is laid before both Houses. The Finance Accounts present the actual receipts and disbursements of the completed year classified under Major Heads.

q: Which of the following correctly distinguishes the Appropriation Act from the Appropriation Accounts of the Railways?

options.A: Both the Appropriation Act and the Appropriation Accounts authorise the withdrawal of moneys from the Consolidated Fund of India
options.B: The Appropriation Act compares the actual expenditure with the Final Grant, whereas the Appropriation Accounts authorise withdrawals from the Consolidated Fund
options.C: The Appropriation Act is prepared after the close of the year by the Accounts Department, whereas the Appropriation Accounts are passed by Parliament before the year begins
options.D: The Appropriation Act is the law which authorises the withdrawal of moneys from the Consolidated Fund of India up to the amounts specified in its Schedule, whereas the Appropriation Accounts, prepared after the close of the year, compare the actual expenditure with the Final Grant and explain the variations between them

e: The Appropriation Act authorises withdrawal of moneys from the Consolidated Fund of India up to the amounts in its Schedule. The Appropriation Accounts, prepared after the year, compare actual expenditure with the Final Grant and explain variations.

q: Which of the following correctly distinguishes the 'Memorandum Explaining the Provisions in the Finance Bill' from the 'Notes on Demands for Grants' presented with the Budget?

options.A: Both the documents explain, clause by clause, the taxation proposals contained in the Finance Bill
options.B: The Memorandum explains, clause by clause, the provisions contained in the Finance Bill, whereas the Notes on Demands for Grants explain the nature, scope and reasons for the significant provisions made in the Demands for Grants
options.C: The Memorandum explains the provisions made in the Demands for Grants, whereas the Notes on Demands for Grants explain the provisions of the Finance Bill
options.D: The Memorandum is presented only to the Rajya Sabha, whereas the Notes on Demands for Grants are presented only to the Lok Sabha

e: The Memorandum Explaining the Provisions in the Finance Bill explains the taxation proposals clause by clause. The Notes on Demands for Grants explain the nature, scope and reasons for significant provisions in the Demands.

q: Which of the following correctly distinguishes the Economic Survey from the Budget document 'Budget at a Glance'?

options.A: Both the documents present the detailed Demands for Grants of the Ministries
options.B: The Economic Survey presents a summary of the Budget figures, whereas 'Budget at a Glance' reviews the state of the economy
options.C: The Economic Survey reviews the state of the economy and is presented shortly before the presentation of the Union Budget, whereas 'Budget at a Glance' presents a brief summary of the Budget, showing the receipts, the expenditure and the various deficit indicators in a nutshell
options.D: The Economic Survey is presented by the Comptroller and Auditor General of India, whereas 'Budget at a Glance' is presented by the Reserve Bank of India

e: The Economic Survey reviews the state of the economy and is presented shortly before the Union Budget. Budget at a Glance summarises the Budget, showing receipts, expenditure and deficit indicators in a nutshell.

q: Which of the following correctly distinguishes the Detailed Demands for Grants of the Ministry of Railways from the 'Notes on Demands for Grants'?

options.A: The Detailed Demands for Grants exhibit the estimates in detail, head-wise, with the figures of the actuals of the previous year and the Budget and Revised Estimates, whereas the Notes on Demands for Grants give brief explanatory notes on the nature, scope and reasons for the significant provisions made in the Demands
options.B: The Detailed Demands for Grants contain only explanatory notes, whereas the Notes on Demands for Grants exhibit the head-wise estimates
options.C: Both the documents contain the detailed classification of Major and Minor Heads of account prescribed in the Finance Code
options.D: The Detailed Demands for Grants are prepared by the zonal railways, whereas the Notes on Demands for Grants are prepared by the Audit Department

e: The Detailed Demands for Grants exhibit estimates in detail head-wise with previous year actuals and Budget and Revised Estimates. The Notes on Demands give brief explanations of the nature, scope and reasons for significant provisions.

q: Which of the following correctly distinguishes a Cash Remittance Note from the bank scroll in railway accounts?

options.A: Both the documents are daily statements rendered by the accredited bank to the Accounts Office
options.B: A Cash Remittance Note is rendered by the bank to the station, whereas the bank scroll accompanies the cash remitted by a station
options.C: A Cash Remittance Note is a register maintained in the Traffic Accounts Office, whereas the bank scroll is a register maintained at the station
options.D: A Cash Remittance Note is the document which accompanies the earnings remitted by a station to the Cash Office or the bank, whereas the bank scroll is the daily statement of receipts and payments rendered by the accredited bank to the Accounts Office, from which the bank's transactions are reconciled with the railway books

e: A Cash Remittance Note accompanies earnings remitted by a station to the Cash Office or bank. The bank scroll is the daily statement of receipts and payments rendered by the accredited bank, used for reconciling bank transactions with railway books.

q: Which of the following correctly distinguishes the Station Balance Sheet from a Cash Remittance Note?

options.A: Both the documents accompany the daily remittance of earnings by a station
options.B: The Station Balance Sheet is the monthly statement rendered by a station to the Traffic Accounts Office, accounting for all the traffic transactions of the station and showing the balance due from the station, whereas a Cash Remittance Note is the document which accompanies the earnings remitted by a station to the Cash Office or the bank
options.C: The Station Balance Sheet accompanies the cash remitted by a station, whereas a Cash Remittance Note is the monthly account of the station
options.D: The Station Balance Sheet is prepared by the Cash Office, whereas a Cash Remittance Note is prepared by the Traffic Accounts Office

e: The Station Balance Sheet is the monthly statement by a station to the Traffic Accounts Office accounting for all its traffic transactions and showing the balance due from it. A Cash Remittance Note only accompanies remitted earnings.

q: Which of the following correctly distinguishes the Traffic Book from the Station Balance Sheet of a railway?

options.A: Both the documents are monthly statements rendered by the stations to the Traffic Accounts Office
options.B: The Traffic Book is the monthly statement of a single station, whereas the Station Balance Sheet deals with the apportionment of earnings among all the railways
options.C: The Traffic Book is the compilation in which the earnings from through traffic are apportioned among the railways over which the traffic has passed, whereas the Station Balance Sheet is the monthly statement rendered by a station to the Traffic Accounts Office, accounting for all the traffic transactions of that station and showing the balance due from it
options.D: The Traffic Book is maintained by the Cash & Pay Office, whereas the Station Balance Sheet is maintained by the Railway Board

e: The Traffic Book is the compilation where through-traffic earnings are apportioned among the railways over which the traffic passed. The Station Balance Sheet is the single station monthly account to the Traffic Accounts Office showing balance due from it.

q: Which of the following correctly distinguishes the Estimates Committee from the Committee on Public Undertakings of Parliament?

options.A: The Estimates Committee examines the estimates of the Ministries with a view to reporting what economies and improvements in organisation and efficiency can be effected consistent with the policy underlying the estimates, whereas the Committee on Public Undertakings examines the reports and accounts of the public undertakings to satisfy itself that their affairs are managed in accordance with sound business principles and prudent commercial practices
options.B: The Estimates Committee examines the accounts of the public undertakings, whereas the Committee on Public Undertakings examines the estimates of the Ministries
options.C: Both the Committees examine the Appropriation Accounts on the basis of the audit reports of the Comptroller and Auditor General
options.D: The Estimates Committee consists of members of both Houses, whereas the Committee on Public Undertakings consists of members of the Lok Sabha alone

e: The Estimates Committee examines Ministry estimates to report economies and improvements in organisation and efficiency consistent with policy. The Committee on Public Undertakings examines public undertaking accounts for sound business principles and prudent commercial practices.

q: Which of the following correctly distinguishes the Public Accounts Committee from the Committee on Public Undertakings of Parliament?

options.A: Both the Committees examine only the reports and accounts of the public undertakings
options.B: The Public Accounts Committee examines the reports and accounts of the public undertakings, whereas the Committee on Public Undertakings examines the Appropriation Accounts of the Ministries
options.C: The Public Accounts Committee consists of members of the Rajya Sabha alone, whereas the Committee on Public Undertakings consists of members of the Lok Sabha alone
options.D: The Public Accounts Committee examines the Appropriation Accounts and the audit reports of the Comptroller and Auditor General thereon, in order to satisfy itself that the moneys disbursed were legally available for, and were applied to, the services and purposes for which Parliament granted them, whereas the Committee on Public Undertakings examines the reports and accounts of the public undertakings, including the railway public sector undertakings

e: The Public Accounts Committee checks that disbursed moneys were legally available for and applied to the purposes granted, using Appropriation Accounts and CAG reports. The Committee on Public Undertakings examines reports and accounts of public undertakings.

q: Which of the following correctly distinguishes the Public Accounts Committee from the Departmentally Related Standing Committee on Railways?

options.A: Both the Committees examine the Demands for Grants before they are voted by the Lok Sabha
options.B: The Public Accounts Committee examines, after the expenditure has been incurred, the Appropriation Accounts and the audit reports thereon, whereas the Departmentally Related Standing Committee on Railways examines the Demands for Grants of the Ministry of Railways before they are voted and presents a report which is recommendatory in character
options.C: The Public Accounts Committee votes the Demands for Grants after examination, whereas the Standing Committee regularises the excess expenditure of past years
options.D: The Public Accounts Committee is a committee of the Rajya Sabha alone, whereas the Standing Committee on Railways is a committee of the Lok Sabha alone

e: The Public Accounts Committee works after expenditure, on Appropriation Accounts and audit reports. The Standing Committee on Railways examines the Railway Demands before they are voted and its report is only recommendatory.

q: Which of the following correctly distinguishes a 'policy cut' motion from an 'economy cut' motion moved on a Demand for Grant in the Lok Sabha?

options.A: Both the motions propose that the Demand be reduced by a nominal sum of one hundred rupees
options.B: A policy cut proposes a reduction of the Demand by a specified amount, whereas an economy cut proposes that the Demand be reduced to one rupee
options.C: A policy cut proposes that the Demand be reduced to one rupee, in order to express disapproval of the policy underlying the Demand, whereas an economy cut proposes that the Demand be reduced by a specified amount, representing the economy that can be effected in the expenditure covered by the Demand
options.D: A policy cut can be moved only on a charged item, whereas an economy cut can be moved only in the Rajya Sabha

e: A policy cut proposes reducing the Demand to one rupee to disapprove the policy behind it. An economy cut proposes reduction by a specified amount representing the economy that can be effected in the Demand.

q: Which of the following correctly distinguishes 'Cheques and Bills' from 'Remittances into Banks' in railway accounts?

options.A: 'Cheques and Bills' is operated for cheques and bills received and deposited with the bank, pending their realisation, and for cheques issued by the Railways, whereas 'Remittances into Banks' is operated for the earnings and other amounts remitted into the bank, pending credit by the bank
options.B: 'Cheques and Bills' is operated for the earnings remitted into the bank, whereas 'Remittances into Banks' is operated for the cheques deposited with the bank
options.C: Both the heads record the transactions of the Railways with the Pay and Accounts Offices of other Ministries
options.D: 'Cheques and Bills' represents amounts due from stations on traffic transactions, whereas 'Remittances into Banks' represents the deposits received from contractors

e: Cheques and Bills covers cheques and bills received and deposited with the bank pending realisation, and cheques issued. Remittances into Banks covers earnings and other amounts remitted into the bank pending credit by the bank.

q: Which of the following correctly distinguishes the capital component from the interest component of the lease charges payable by the Railways to the Indian Railway Finance Corporation?

options.A: Both the components are charged to revenue as part of the working expenses of the Railways
options.B: The capital component is recovered from the Depreciation Reserve Fund, whereas the interest component is charged to Capital
options.C: The capital component is treated as a deposit with the Corporation, whereas the interest component is treated as a loan to it
options.D: The capital component is accounted for as capital outlay under the Plan Head for Leased Assets, whereas the interest component, being a finance charge, is charged to revenue as part of the working expenses of the Railways

e: For IRFC leased assets, the capital component of lease charges is accounted as capital outlay under the Plan Head for Leased Assets, while the interest component, a finance charge, is charged to revenue as working expenses.
